narrative:
The model estimated a 43% chance that you would be a bad credit risk. Although that is below a coin-flip, it was high enough under the bank’s lending rule to decline this application. The decision was not driven by your age, sex or foreign-worker status.

The most influential factor was the amount of credit you requested. At 3,804 DM, this factor was the strongest in the assessment, but it actually worked in your favour, pushing the prediction toward good credit rather than bad. The denial was therefore driven mainly by the next two factors. Your checking-account status, 0–200 DM, pushed toward bad credit; among approved applicants, most have no checking-account information recorded (59.2%), while only 18.4% fall in your 0–200 DM range. Your credit history—no credits/all paid—also pushed toward bad credit, and it is uncommon among approved applicants: only 1.0% share it, compared with 57.3% who have existing paid credit. Together, these two factors outweighed the favourable amount signal.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your banking and credit profile: avoid overdrafts, build a steadier checking-account balance, and establish a track record of repaid credit rather than having no credit history. Ask the lender what specific evidence would support a successful reapplication, and consider reapplying after those records improve.
